A2 Touring: No Compromise Needed

The A2 motorcycle licence restricts riders to machines producing no more than 47bhp with a power-to-weight ratio not exceeding 0.2kW/kg. While this rules out the big adventure bikes and sport tourers, it does not prevent genuinely enjoyable UK touring. Several A2-legal bikes are purpose-built for touring and can carry you comfortably across the entire country.

A2 Licence Rules Explained

You can ride any bike up to 47bhp, or a bike originally producing up to 94bhp that has been restricted to 47bhp. This opens up a surprisingly wide range of machines. Most manufacturers offer A2-compliant versions of their popular models, either natively or with an ECU restriction that can be removed when you upgrade to a full licence.

Best A2 Touring Bikes 2026

Honda CB500X — The gold standard A2 tourer. Natively A2-compliant at 47bhp, it needs no restriction kit. The 471cc parallel twin is smooth and economical. At 199kg it is manageable for newer riders. Comfortable ergonomics suit all-day riding and the aftermarket support for luggage is extensive.

Kawasaki Versys 650 (restricted) — The 650 twin restricted to 47bhp retains excellent touring character. Comfortable riding position, good wind protection with the optional taller screen, and a proven, reliable engine.

Yamaha Tracer 7 (restricted) — The CP2 twin restricted from 72bhp to 47bhp still feels lively and engaging. The Tracer platform adds touring comfort and the styling is sharp. One of the most popular A2 tourers for good reason.

Suzuki V-Strom 650 (restricted) — The evergreen V-Strom is an outstanding A2 tourer. Comfortable, reliable, economical, and blessed with an enormous owner community. Budget-friendly too.

Royal Enfield Himalayan 450 — Natively A2-compliant at approximately 40bhp. The new Himalayan is light, simple, and adventure-capable. It will not win any speed contests but for exploring Britain's back roads and green lanes, it is ideal.

Touring on 47bhp

  • Motorway capability — All these bikes handle motorways comfortably at legal speeds. Overtaking requires more planning than on unrestricted machines but is perfectly manageable.
  • Hill climbing — A2 bikes handle British hills without issue. Lower gears and the torque characteristics of twins and singles provide adequate pull even on steep Highland passes.
  • Loaded performance — Adding 20-30kg of luggage is noticeable but not problematic. Keep luggage light and you will barely feel the difference.
Do not wish away your A2 years. Some riders look back on their A2 touring as the most enjoyable riding of their lives. A lighter, less powerful bike forces you to develop better riding skills and appreciate every road more.
keyTakeaways: The A2 licence limits you to 47bhp with a power-to-weight ratio no higher than 0.2kW/kg.
You can ride a native 47bhp bike or a bike up to 94bhp restricted down to the limit.
The Honda CB500X is the gold-standard A2 tourer, natively compliant with no restrictor needed.
All the leading A2 tourers handle motorways, hills and light luggage comfortably at legal speeds.
A restrictor kit can often be removed later when you gain your full licence.

faq.q: What are the A2 licence power rules?
faq.a: The A2 licence restricts you to motorcycles producing no more than 47bhp with a power-to-weight ratio not exceeding 0.2kW/kg. You can ride any bike that meets this natively, or a bike originally producing up to 94bhp that has been restricted down to 47bhp. Most manufacturers offer A2-compliant versions of popular models, either from the factory or via an ECU restrictor.

Yes. All the leading A2 tourers handle motorways comfortably at legal speeds and climb British hills, including steep Highland passes, without issue thanks to the torque of twins and singles. Overtaking simply needs more planning than on an unrestricted bike. Adding 20 to 30kg of luggage is noticeable but not problematic if you pack light, so genuine UK touring is well within reach.

faq.q: Is the Honda CB500X the best A2 tourer?
faq.a: It is the benchmark. The CB500X is natively A2-compliant at 47bhp so needs no restrictor kit, its 471cc parallel twin is smooth and economical, and at 199kg it is manageable for newer riders. Comfortable all-day ergonomics and huge aftermarket luggage support round it out. Restricted rivals like the Tracer 7 and V-Strom 650 are also excellent alternatives.

faq.q: Can I remove the restrictor when I get my full licence?
faq.a: On most restricted bikes, yes. Bikes that were derestricted from a higher output, such as the Tracer 7 or Tenere 700, can have the ECU restriction removed once you hold a full licence, unlocking their full power. Native 47bhp bikes like the CB500X have no restrictor to remove. Always have the work done properly and inform your insurer of any change.
